column6: Isaiah tells the righteous they will eat the fruit of their deeds; this is a direct good-work counterpart to the commentary's final division and recompense.
The next verse says the wicked will receive what their own hands have done; it supplies the adverse half of the commentary's work-by-work settlement.
Hosea says the people forget that God remembers their evil, while their deeds now surround them and stand before him; this closely matches the commentary's deeds found present at the account.
Elihu says God repays a person for work and causes each to find the consequence of a way; this states the commentary's personal work-to-recompense formula in another setting.

column5: eyes on all ways and deeds
column6: Jeremiah praises God's eyes upon all human ways so as to give each according to conduct and the fruit of deeds; this joins the commentary's complete record to individual repayment.

Ezekiel denies that child or parent bears the other's guilt and assigns each one's righteousness or wickedness to that person; this specifies the commentary's every-person account as individually owned.

Ezekiel says a turning sinner's former transgressions will not be remembered when he lives by righteousness; this qualifies the commentary's image of every past deed remaining present in the final record.

The psalm's qualified guest walks blamelessly, does righteousness, and speaks truth in the heart; this combines good action and truth as the surah's exception does, with access to God's dwelling as its outcome.

column5: books of sins and stored righteousness
column6: The apocalypse places written sins beside treasuries of righteous deeds when judgment arrives; this develops the commentary's present records and divided good and bad acts into two kinds of stored evidence.

The apocalyptic description says works follow, reward appears, good deeds awaken, and wicked deeds do not sleep; this gives the commentary's acts found present at judgment a vivid independent formulation.

column5: recompense at death according to conduct
column6: Sirach says it is easy for the Lord to repay a person at death according to that person's ways; this joins the commentary's allotted term and binding individual recompense.
A voice says those who die in the Lord rest from labors and their works follow them; this closely meets the commentary's time limit, enduring good works, and deeds present afterward.

column5: doers of good and evil rise differently
column6: Jesus says those who have done good rise to life and those who have done evil to judgment; this makes the commentary's good and bad deeds decisive at the final separation.
James says faith by itself is dead if it has no works; this gives the surah's pairing of belief and righteous deeds a specific consequence when action is absent.
Jesus tells threatened disciples they will gain their lives through endurance; this sets patient perseverance directly opposite the commentary's human loss.

column5: endure to end and be saved
column6: The hated disciple who endures to the end will be saved; this joins the surah's patience to the commentary's deadline and exception from loss.
The risen speaker tells Sardis that its works have not been found complete before God; this is a precise counterpart to the commentary's apparently good work that fails the final assessment.

column5: impartial judgment of each one's work
column6: Peter says the Father judges impartially according to each person's work and tells believers to conduct themselves in reverent fear during their time away; this joins personal deeds, just measurement, and a limited present term.
Hebrews says endurance is needed so that, after doing God's will, the hearers may receive the promise; this links good action and patience to a future recompense.
Jesus adds that one's own words will justify or condemn; this gives the commentary's exact accounting an explicit verdict for the small speech acts named in the preceding verse.
Jesus says entry into the kingdom belongs to one doing his Father's will, which explains why the impressive acts claimed in the following verse can still fail the commentary's good-work test.
The rejected did not feed the hungry or give drink to the thirsty; this supplies the negative half of the commentary's smallest deed carrying weight at the division.
The speaker says he searches mind and heart and will give each person according to works; this adds the inward quality of deeds to the commentary's personal final account.
Daniel's third explanation says Belshazzar's kingdom is divided and given away; it specifies what is lost when the weighed account in the preceding verse proves deficient.

Proverbs contrasts gain from labor with need arising from mere talk, using the table's Hebrew lack root; this is a present-life analogue to the commentary's work and loss account, not an end-time verdict.

column5: Hebrew חקק in decree; table sound correspondence
column6: Zephaniah urges action before the decree takes effect and before the Lord's angry day arrives; this places a prescribed term beside the commentary's appointed judgment day, while the root link remains unverified.

After the fruitful righteous person, the psalm depicts wicked people as chaff driven away by wind; this supplies a contrasting failure of substance beside the commentary's separated losers, without asserting a literal scale.

The apocalyptic court opens books of the living before the divine presence; this develops the commentary's record-and-day scene, though the books concern those counted as living rather than a list of every act.
Ephesians explicitly denies that salvation arises from works, complicating a reading of the commentary's good deeds as the basis of rescue from loss.
The next verse says believers are made for good works prepared for them to walk in; this preserves good action alongside the preceding grace claim and the surah's believing doers.
Paul says faith works through love; this gives the surah's paired belief and action a concrete communal form rather than treating faith as mere assent.
Peter says the Lord's apparent delay expresses patience so people may repent; this gives the commentary's appointed day a different role for patience, allowing change before the account closes.
The rejected ask when they failed to serve the king in his needs; their surprise is a concrete instance of the commentary's people who misjudge the worth of their own conduct.
The Laodiceans claim to need nothing but are called poor and exposed; this supplies the commentary's self-mistaken assessment with a striking deficit image.
Jesus says greater trust brings a greater demand; this is a specific proportional-account rule beside the commentary's precise weighing of each person's acts.
Paul promises relief to the afflicted when the Lord is revealed; this completes the reversal of affliction and repayment in the surrounding judgment passage and the commentary's righteous exception.

Augustine discusses the books opened at the last judgment as a disclosure of what people have done, possibly through divine recall rather than physical ledgers; this changes how the commentary's visible account can be imagined.

column5: qere לו; deeds measured by God
column6: In Hannah's song the traditional qere makes God the one by whom deeds are measured, closely matching the commentary's scales for human action; WLC's written ketiv ולא differs, so this connection depends on the named reading.

column5: WLC ketiv ולא versus qere לו
column6: The written ketiv can be read as denying that deeds are measured, unlike the commentary's scales; the familiar qere gives the opposite sense, so the reversal is textually uncertain and should be checked against the WLC stream.

A scene in this recension appears to bring a soul's merits and sins into a heavenly weighing, close to the commentary's personal balance; the chapter placement and the roles of the heavenly figures are uncertain from memory.
